title: Nurtec and Alcohol: Can You Drink on Rimegepant?
excerpt: Can you drink on Nurtec? There's no known direct interaction with rimegepant, but alcohol is a common migraine trigger. Here's how to time it, what to avoid, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Nurtec? There's no known direct interaction, but alcohol is a common migraine trigger. Timing, wine, other meds, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no known direct interaction between Nurtec ODT (rimegepant) and alcohol. The drug's prescribing information doesn't carry an alcohol warning, and the two are broken down by mostly different routes in the body. For most people with migraine, a single drink on a day they've used Nurtec is unlikely to cause a dangerous reaction. The real problem is the other direction: alcohol is one of the most common migraine triggers, it worsens the nausea and dehydration that come with an attack, and drinking during or right after an attack can bring the pain back. So the question is less "is it dangerous?" and more "is it working against my treatment?"

**The quick rules:** Don't drink to "take the edge off" a migraine. Wait until an attack has fully cleared before having alcohol. If you take Nurtec every other day for prevention, ask your doctor how alcohol fits your plan, and watch whether drinking days are followed by migraine days. Don't take more than one 75 mg dose in 24 hours. Check any other painkiller you add, because those are the medicines where alcohol warnings actually apply. And ask your doctor or pharmacist how alcohol fits with everything else you take.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and full medication list. **Talk to your doctor before combining Nurtec with alcohol if** you have liver or kidney disease, high blood pressure, Raynaud's phenomenon, you take other migraine medicines or medicines that affect liver enzymes, or you drink most days. **Get medical help right away if** you notice swelling of the face, lips, or throat, trouble breathing, or a widespread rash after taking Nurtec, or if you have a sudden "worst headache of your life," a headache with weakness, numbness, confusion, trouble speaking, fever, or a stiff neck. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Nurtec Is and How It Works

Nurtec ODT is the brand name for **rimegepant**, a migraine medicine taken as a 75 mg tablet that dissolves on or under the tongue. It belongs to a class called **gepants**, which block the receptor for a protein called CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide). CGRP is released by nerves around the brain's blood vessels during a migraine attack and plays a central role in the pain and inflammation of the attack. By blocking its receptor, rimegepant helps stop the attack from building.

Nurtec is approved in the US for two uses in adults:

1. **Acute treatment** of a migraine attack, with or without aura. You take one dose when the attack starts.
2. **Preventive treatment** of episodic migraine, taken as one dose every other day.

The label caps use at one 75 mg dose in 24 hours. That matters for drinkers, because a migraine that comes back after a night out can tempt people to take a second tablet sooner than they should.

Gepants work differently from triptans such as sumatriptan. Triptans narrow blood vessels, which is why they're avoided in people with certain heart and circulation problems. Rimegepant doesn't work mainly by constricting vessels, which is one reason it's an option for some people who can't take triptans. That difference doesn't change the alcohol picture much, but it helps explain why the alcohol advice for Nurtec is mostly about triggers rather than chemistry.

## Is There a Direct Interaction Between Nurtec and Alcohol?

As far as published information goes, no. The prescribing information for Nurtec ODT lists interactions with medicines that affect certain liver enzymes, but alcohol isn't among them, and there is no formal warning against drinking. Here's the plain-words reason why the two don't appear to clash.

**How your body clears rimegepant.** Rimegepant is broken down mainly by a liver enzyme called **CYP3A4**, with a smaller contribution from another enzyme called CYP2C9. It's also moved around the body by a transporter called P-glycoprotein. The label tells people to avoid Nurtec with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (medicines that block that enzyme and push drug levels up), to avoid taking a second dose within 48 hours when on a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor, and to avoid strong or moderate CYP3A4 inducers (medicines that speed the enzyme up and can make Nurtec less effective).

**How your body clears alcohol.** Alcohol is mostly broken down by a different enzyme, alcohol dehydrogenase, and then by aldehyde dehydrogenase. In people who drink heavily over time, another enzyme called CYP2E1 picks up more of the load. None of these are the main enzyme that handles rimegepant. So there's no clear reason to expect a normal amount of alcohol to raise or lower rimegepant levels in a meaningful way.

**What we don't know.** "No known interaction" is not the same as "studied and cleared." There's no large clinical trial that deliberately gave people Nurtec and alcohol together and measured the results. Most guidance on this comes from understanding how each substance is processed, plus the absence of reported problems. That's reassuring for occasional, moderate drinking, but it isn't a green light for heavy drinking.

**Where long-term drinking does matter.** Nurtec is not recommended for people with severe liver impairment, and the label advises avoiding it in people with end-stage kidney disease. Years of heavy drinking can damage the liver. If that's a possibility for you, your doctor needs to know before prescribing or continuing Nurtec.

## The Bigger Issue: Alcohol Is a Common Migraine Trigger

This is the part of the "Nurtec and alcohol" question that matters most day to day. Alcohol is one of the most frequently reported migraine triggers. A large Dutch survey of people with migraine, published in the *European Journal of Neurology*, found that roughly a third named alcohol as a trigger, and red wine was the drink most often blamed. The same research noted that many people with migraine drink less than the general population, likely because they've learned the hard way.

The international headache classification used by doctors recognizes two kinds of alcohol-related headache:

- **Immediate alcohol-induced headache**, which starts within about three hours of drinking (sometimes called a "cocktail headache").
- **Delayed alcohol-induced headache**, which shows up the next morning as alcohol levels fall. This is close to what most people call a hangover headache.

People with migraine are more prone to both, and in them a drink can set off a full migraine attack rather than just a dull ache. Researchers have several ideas about why alcohol triggers attacks, and it's likely a mix:

- **Blood vessel effects.** Alcohol widens blood vessels, and some people's migraine pathways seem sensitive to that change.
- **Dehydration.** Alcohol increases urine output, and dehydration is a well-known headache trigger on its own.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night. Sleep disruption is one of the strongest migraine triggers.
- **Other ingredients.** Red wine contains compounds such as tannins, histamine, and other plant chemicals that some researchers suspect play a role. Sulfites often get blamed, but the evidence for them as a migraine trigger is weaker than many people assume. Our guides on [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) and [sulfites in wine](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) go deeper.
- **Acetaldehyde.** The toxic breakdown product of alcohol builds up after heavy drinking and contributes to hangover symptoms, including headache.

So even though Nurtec and alcohol don't interact chemically, drinking can create the very attack you're trying to treat or prevent. Our full guide to [migraine after drinking](/never-hungover/migraine-after-drinking) covers patterns and prevention in more detail.

## Nurtec and Wine: Does the Type of Drink Matter?

People search for "Nurtec and wine" more than any other drink, and it makes sense. Red wine has the strongest reputation as a migraine trigger. Being on Nurtec doesn't change that reputation, because the medicine doesn't block the trigger itself; it blocks part of the pain process once the attack starts.

What the evidence and patient experience suggest:

- **Red wine** is the drink most often reported as a trigger, though plenty of people with migraine tolerate it fine. Triggers are personal.
- **White wine, clear spirits, and lighter beers** are reported as triggers less often, but they aren't trigger-free. Any alcohol can contribute to dehydration and poor sleep.
- **Amount usually matters more than type.** Many people find one drink is fine while two or three is not.
- **Timing matters too.** Drinking when you're already tired, stressed, hungry, or close to your period (for people with menstrual migraine) stacks triggers on top of each other.

One small practical note: grapefruit juice is known to block CYP3A4, the main enzyme that clears rimegepant. Grapefruit isn't specifically named in the Nurtec label, and an occasional cocktail with a splash of it probably isn't a big deal, but if you drink grapefruit-based cocktails or juice often, it's worth asking your pharmacist.

## Can You Drink on Nurtec for Prevention (Every-Other-Day Dosing)?

If you take Nurtec every other day to prevent episodic migraine, you're on it most of the time, so "should I drink on Nurtec?" becomes "can I drink at all?" The short answer is that there's no known interaction, so moderate drinking isn't ruled out by the medicine itself. Many people on preventive treatment have an occasional drink.

The more useful question is whether drinking is undoing the prevention. A preventive medicine is meant to reduce how many migraine days you have. If alcohol triggers attacks for you, regular drinking can make the medicine look like it's working less well than it really is. Some ways to keep an eye on this:

- **Keep a headache diary** that records drinks, sleep, stress, food, and migraine days. Many people use a phone app for this.
- **Look for a 24-hour pattern.** If migraine days often follow drinking days, that's a strong clue.
- **Test one change at a time.** For example, skip red wine for a month and see whether your migraine count changes.
- **Bring the diary to your doctor.** It's the best information they have for deciding whether your treatment is working.

Some other preventive migraine medicines do have real alcohol concerns. If you take Nurtec alongside a different preventive, check that medicine separately. For example, our guides on [topiramate and alcohol](/never-hungover/topiramate-and-alcohol) and [propranolol and alcohol](/never-hungover/propranolol-and-alcohol) cover two common ones where alcohol can add to side effects such as dizziness, drowsiness, or low blood pressure.

## How Long After Taking Nurtec Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period, because no direct interaction has been found. But that doesn't mean the timing is meaningless. A few things to keep in mind:

**Rimegepant lasts a while.** Its half-life is roughly 11 hours, meaning it takes about that long for half the drug to clear. It's still in your system the next day. That's fine on its own, but it means "waiting until it's gone" isn't a realistic goal, and there's no need to try.

**Wait for the attack to resolve.** The most practical rule is to hold off on alcohol until the migraine has completely cleared, not just eased. Drinking during the tail end of an attack is a common way to bring it back.

**Rehydrate and eat first.** Migraine attacks often come with nausea, poor appetite, and skipped meals. Alcohol on an empty, dehydrated stomach is more likely to trigger trouble.

**Remember the 24-hour limit.** If your migraine returns after drinking, you can't simply take another Nurtec. The label limits use to one dose in 24 hours. Ask your doctor in advance what your backup plan should be for an attack that comes back.

## What If You Drank and Then Got a Migraine?

This is one of the most common real-world situations: a night out, then a migraine the next morning. If you have a migraine diagnosis and your doctor has prescribed Nurtec for attacks, many clinicians would want you to treat an alcohol-triggered migraine like any other attack, early and at the labeled dose. The medicine doesn't care what set the attack off.

That said, a few cautions:

- **Not every next-morning headache is a migraine.** A hangover headache in someone without migraine is a different problem. Nurtec isn't approved or studied as a hangover treatment, and it shouldn't be borrowed from a friend for one.
- **Know your own attack pattern.** Migraine usually has features such as one-sided throbbing pain, sensitivity to light or sound, nausea, or aura. A dull, all-over ache with thirst and fatigue sounds more like a hangover. Ask your doctor how to tell the two apart for you.
- **Look after the hangover parts too.** Water, an electrolyte drink, food, and rest help with dehydration and low blood sugar that can keep a headache going. Our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers the practical steps.
- **Don't keep drinking.** "Hair of the dog" delays the hangover and can feed another attack.

## Nurtec With Other Pain Relievers When You've Been Drinking

People often combine Nurtec with an over-the-counter pain reliever, especially for a stubborn attack. Whether that's appropriate for you is a question for your prescriber. But if you do, the add-on medicine is usually where the real alcohol warnings live.

- **Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs).** The US labels warn that people who have 3 or more alcoholic drinks a day face a higher risk of stomach bleeding. Alcohol already irritates the stomach lining. Take NSAIDs with food and water, stay within the label dose, and avoid them after a heavy night if you can. See our guides on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol).
- **Excedrin and other acetaminophen combinations.** Excedrin Migraine combines acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine. Acetaminophen and heavy drinking together can strain the liver, and the aspirin adds stomach-bleeding risk. Our [Excedrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/excedrin-and-alcohol) guide explains the details.
- **Triptans.** Some people use both a triptan and a gepant. Alcohol doesn't have a strong known interaction with triptans either (our guide to [sumatriptan and alcohol](/never-hungover/sumatriptan-and-alcohol) covers the most common one), but combining migraine medicines is something to plan with your doctor, not improvise after a night out.
- **Sleep aids and antihistamines.** Many "PM" products contain sedating antihistamines. Alcohol increases drowsiness and dizziness from these, which is a bigger practical risk than anything to do with Nurtec.

The general rule: **one medicine at a time, at the label dose, and ask a pharmacist before stacking products**, especially if you've been drinking.

## Side Effects to Know About

Nurtec is generally well tolerated in clinical trials. Knowing its side effects helps you tell what's the medicine and what's the alcohol.

**Nausea** was the most common side effect in the trials for acute treatment. In the prevention trial, nausea along with stomach pain or indigestion were among the more common ones. Alcohol can make nausea and stomach upset worse, so drinking soon after a dose may make you feel worse even without any chemical interaction.

**Allergic (hypersensitivity) reactions** are uncommon but can be serious. The label notes reactions such as shortness of breath and rash, and that they can happen days after a dose. Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing, needs emergency care.

**High blood pressure** has been reported in people taking CGRP-blocking medicines, including new high blood pressure and worsening of existing high blood pressure. Heavy drinking also raises blood pressure over time, so if you drink regularly and take Nurtec, it's reasonable to have your blood pressure checked.

**Raynaud's phenomenon**, where fingers or toes turn white or blue and numb in the cold, has also been reported with CGRP-blocking medicines. Tell your doctor if you notice it.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

For a social drinker who has a glass of wine on a Nurtec day, a medical emergency is very unlikely. But some symptoms need prompt care no matter what you've taken.

> **Call 911 or go to an emergency room if you have:** swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing; a sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache that peaks within a minute; a headache with weakness, numbness, drooping face, confusion, or trouble speaking; a headache with fever and a stiff neck; or a headache after a head injury (falls are more common after drinking). **Contact your doctor soon if** your migraine pattern changes noticeably, attacks become more frequent, you need acute medicine more and more often, you notice new high blood pressure or color changes in your fingers or toes, or you have a rash after taking Nurtec. **If you're unsure about a possible medicine mix-up**, US Poison Control is available 24/7 at **1-800-222-1222**.

A new or very different headache shouldn't be written off as "just a hangover" or "just my migraine." When in doubt, get checked.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

The general advice above fits most adults with migraine who drink occasionally and moderately. These groups should talk to their doctor before drinking on Nurtec:

- **People with liver disease or who drink heavily on a regular basis.** Nurtec is not recommended in severe liver impairment, and heavy drinking can damage the liver.
- **People with serious kidney disease.** The label advises avoiding Nurtec in end-stage kidney disease.
- **People who take medicines that affect CYP3A4.** This includes some antifungals, some antibiotics, some HIV and heart medicines, and some seizure medicines. These interactions are with the medicines, not alcohol, but people often don't think to mention them.
- **People with high blood pressure or Raynaud's phenomenon.**
- **People who are pregnant, trying to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.** Alcohol isn't recommended in pregnancy, and the decision about Nurtec needs a doctor's input.
- **People on several sedating medicines.** Alcohol adds to drowsiness from many other drugs.

## A Better Path: Fewer Triggers, Not Just Faster Treatment

Nurtec treats or helps prevent migraine attacks, but it doesn't remove the triggers. If alcohol regularly sets off your attacks, the most effective step is usually the simplest one: drink less, drink slower, and make sure you're eating and staying hydrated. Some habits that help many people with migraine:

- **Set a limit before you start.** One drink is often well tolerated where two or three are not.
- **Alternate every drink with a glass of water.**
- **Eat a real meal first**, so you're not drinking on an empty stomach.
- **Protect your sleep.** Finish drinking a few hours before bed and keep a regular wake-up time.
- **Avoid stacking triggers.** Skip drinking on days you're already short on sleep, stressed, or close to a known trigger window.
- **Swap the drink, not the occasion.** If red wine is a reliable trigger, try a different drink or a low- or no-alcohol option.

Our guides on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) and [why alcohol causes headaches](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) explain the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also look at supplements. Here's an honest view of one we cover often:

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents alcohol-triggered migraines, and it is not a migraine treatment or a substitute for Nurtec. It also hasn't been studied in combination with rimegepant, so if you'd like to try it, mention it to your doctor or pharmacist first. Some readers who drink socially use it as part of their routine; popular picks include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) and [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) cover how much people take and what to check first.

One last rule: no supplement should change how you use your migraine medicine. Follow your prescriber's plan and the 24-hour dosing limit, whatever else you take.

## The Bottom Line

- There's **no known direct interaction** between Nurtec (rimegepant) and alcohol, and the label doesn't carry an alcohol warning.
- Rimegepant and alcohol are processed mostly by **different liver enzymes**, but the combination hasn't been formally studied, so moderation still matters.
- The real concern is that **alcohol is a common migraine trigger**, especially red wine, and drinking can bring on or prolong the attacks Nurtec is treating or preventing.
- **Wait until an attack has fully cleared** before drinking, and remember the limit of one 75 mg dose in 24 hours.
- If you add a pain reliever, **that's where the alcohol warnings are**: NSAIDs and stomach bleeding, acetaminophen and the liver.
- Talk to your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, high blood pressure, take other medicines that affect CYP3A4, or drink most days.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Nurtec?**

There is no known direct drug interaction between Nurtec ODT (rimegepant) and alcohol, and the prescribing information does not include an alcohol warning. That doesn't mean drinking is a good idea during a migraine attack: alcohol is a common migraine trigger, it can worsen nausea and dehydration, and it may make the attack harder to treat. If your doctor says an occasional drink is fine, keep it small, drink water alongside it, and ask your doctor or pharmacist how it fits with your other medicines.

**How long after taking Nurtec can I drink alcohol?**

There is no official waiting period, because no interaction between rimegepant and alcohol has been identified. The practical advice is to wait until the migraine has fully resolved, you've eaten, and you're well hydrated. Rimegepant has a half-life of roughly 11 hours, so it stays in your system for a day or more, but the bigger reason to wait is that drinking during or right after an attack can bring the headache back.

**Can I take Nurtec for a hangover headache?**

Nurtec is approved to treat migraine attacks and to help prevent episodic migraine. It is not a hangover remedy. If you have migraine and alcohol set off a genuine migraine attack, your doctor may want you to treat it like any other attack. A plain hangover headache in someone without migraine is a different problem, and Nurtec isn't designed or studied for it. Ask your prescriber how to tell the two apart in your own case.

**Is it safe to drink wine on Nurtec?**

Wine doesn't interact with rimegepant in any known way, but red wine is one of the most commonly reported migraine triggers. If wine tends to set off your attacks, being on Nurtec doesn't change that. Some people find white wine, clear spirits, or simply smaller amounts easier to tolerate. A headache diary is the most reliable way to learn your own pattern.

**Can I drink if I take Nurtec every other day for prevention?**

Many people on preventive Nurtec drink moderately without problems, since there is no known interaction. The catch is that frequent or heavy drinking can trigger attacks and work against the prevention you're trying to achieve. Talk to your doctor about what amount makes sense for you, and track whether drinking days are followed by migraine days.

**Does alcohol make Nurtec less effective?**

There is no good evidence that alcohol changes how rimegepant is absorbed or broken down. Alcohol is processed mostly by different liver enzymes than the one that handles rimegepant (CYP3A4). But if alcohol is triggering or worsening the attack, the medicine may seem to work less well simply because the trigger is still active. Long-term heavy drinking that damages the liver is a different matter, since Nurtec is not recommended in severe liver impairment.

**What side effects of Nurtec could alcohol make worse?**

Nausea is the most common side effect reported for Nurtec, and alcohol can make nausea and stomach upset worse. Alcohol also causes dehydration and poor sleep, both of which can feed a migraine. Nurtec can rarely cause allergic reactions such as rash or trouble breathing, sometimes days after a dose. Those need medical care right away regardless of whether you've been drinking.

**Is it safe to take Nurtec with ibuprofen or Excedrin after drinking?**

Doctors sometimes allow Nurtec alongside a pain reliever, but check with yours first. The bigger alcohol concern is with the add-on: ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin carry stomach-bleeding warnings for people who have 3 or more drinks a day, and Excedrin contains acetaminophen, which strains the liver in heavy drinkers. Stick to label doses, take NSAIDs with food, and don't stack several products without asking a pharmacist.
